source.title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
source.authors: Cheng-Yu Xie; Fei Shen; Shu-Yi Miao; Yue Feng; Jian Yu; Pengyang Shao; Yi-Jun Tian; Xiao-Yu Du

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It contains some garbled text in figure content, but the relevant reported results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It derives safety-related FFN coordinates from safe/unsafe activation statistics and tests their suppression and cross-language activation-state transfer. This is a conceptual test of the causal safety mechanism and its transfer, but it does not project out the original single residual-stream direction.
record.gate_note: The paper reports activation-suppression results for SCAR-selected neuron sets and a safety-state transfer intervention. These are recorded below. SK-Masked LoRA results are not rows for the listed versions: they are safety behavior induced through supervised fine-tuning, not evidence about behavior absent that inducement. The paper also reports individual language results in Figure 3, but the text gives only model-level target-language averages.
record.test_reason: The study derives FFN output coordinates from mean safe/unsafe activation contrasts. Zeroing them sharply raises MultiJail ASR in two instruct models, against matched random controls. Injecting an EN/ZH safe-response state on the shared coordinates lowers ASR in KO/TH/BN. This is a different method (sparse neuron coordinates, not a residual-stream difference-in-means direction) aimed at whether a compact, cross-lingually shared internal component causally mediates refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that a compact, cross-lingually shared set of FFN neurons (the safety kernel) is functionally associated with multilingual safety: suppressing it weakens refusal, and injecting a safe-response state improves it. SK-Masked LoRA lowers ASR, including in unseen languages, with limited capability change.
record.recipe_differences: The paper ranks FFN output coordinates with a SCAR score combining standardized safe/unsafe activation separation and activation shift, then suppresses selected coordinates or injects a source activation state. It does not form and project out a single residual-stream difference-in-means direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The number of candidate neurons k is varied; the text says English suppression begins to stabilize around k = 5000. Discovery-language composition changes SK size, with individual exclusions giving increments from +4.0% (IT) to +17.6% (BN). State transfer uses alpha = 4.
record.problems: The activation-suppression results concern selected neuron-coordinate sets, not the claimed single residual-stream direction. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for these results. General capability measures are reported for SK-Masked LoRA, not for the activation-suppression intervention.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3, Table 4, Table 5, and Figure 4 results for SK-Masked LoRA are omitted because they evaluate safety behavior induced by supervised fine-tuning rather than the claimed direction or its ablation. Table 5 capability scores therefore do not establish capability preservation after the claimed direction is removed.

untested.parts: No single residual-stream difference-in-means direction is projected out. Inducing refusal on harmless prompts by adding a direction is not tested. General capabilities after activation suppression are not measured; MMLU/MGSM are reported only for LoRA variants.
Transfer across model variants and from base to instruct models is not tested. The transfer vector is a safe-response activation mean, not the refusal direction.
No weight-edit abliteration of released models.
No analysis of jailbreaks suppressing the direction, and no adversarial training against ablation.
No comparison of single direction versus multi-dimensional structure.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal.
No reasoning models are examined, and Qwen3 thinking mode is not analyzed.

missing.what: Top-k sweep of ASR increase after English language-wise suppression for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-it. ΔASR grows from about 30-40 to about 60-70 as k rises, and stabilizes around k=5000. This shows the removal effect depends on the selection size.
Per-language before/after ASR for SK state injection in KO, TH and BN for each of the three backbones. The figure is only partly legible in the text.

record.verdict_notes: The construct gap is large. The paper localizes refusal to about 0.12-0.57% of FFN output coordinates (5000 per language), not to one residual-stream direction. V1 rows are therefore indirect evidence that a mean-difference-derived component causally mediates refusal; they neither confirm nor refute the 'single direction' part. The Table 1 random controls are noisy for Llama (KO +10.5, BN -19.7), which weakens the BN contrast. SK-Masked LoRA results (Tables 3-5) are correctly excluded as induced safety behavior. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: It does not project out a single difference-in-means direction, test adding that direction on harmless requests, or assess general capabilities after activation suppression. The intervention instead suppresses sets of FFN output coordinates.
No weight edit converting ablation into released-model abliteration is tested.
No attack is tested for suppressing the claimed direction, and no training against its ablation is tested.
The paper identifies sets of neuron coordinates, but does not compare a single direction with an affine subspace, cone, or dominant direction plus other directions.
No separation between harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is tested.
The study tests transfer of an activation state across languages, not transfer across model variants or from base to instruct models.
No comparison of how or when refusal training determines whether a single removable direction exists.
No reasoning models are evaluated for V1.

relationships.reason: Suppression raises ASR to 69-81% against near-default random controls, but 19-31% of harmful prompts are still refused (r02-r24, r27, r30). Removal is substantial but incomplete.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Zeroing SCAR-selected language-wise sets or the SK in Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-it, MultiJail, GPT-4o judge
source_check.reason: Values are right: Table 1 gives 69.52-81.27, and Table 2's SK averages are 69.05 and 71.64. The authors call this 'weakens' safe refusal, which is incomplete removal. The reason's '19-31% still refused' goes beyond the text: ASR is GPT-4o-judged attack success, and the text never says the non-successes are refusals. Llama's per-language random controls are not all near default (KO 40.95 vs 30.47, BN 46.03 vs 65.71); only the averages are. Capability under suppression is untested, so it is not a scope limit. The object is a coordinate set, not a direction.

relationships.condition: SK coordinates shared across six languages (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-it), and EN/ZH state injection into KO/TH/BN (Qwen3-8B, Gemma-2-9B-it)

relationships.display_finding: Suppressing shared safety coordinates raised average ASR by 45–53 percentage points, while English/Chinese state injection lowered target ASR from 20.21 to 11.96 in Qwen3 and 5.18 to 3.17 in Gemma.

relation.reason: Its own suppression experiments (with matched random controls) and state-injection experiments report ASR changes bearing on V1 and V6, though only via neuron coordinates. Arditi et al. [1] and Wang et al. [32] are cited only in related work.

tranche.reason: It ranks and zeroes FFN output coordinates using standardized safe/unsafe mean contrasts, and adds a mean safe-response state. This is a different method on whether a contrast-derived component causally mediates refusal and carries across languages. No difference-in-means direction is computed or ablated.

source_check.notes: The record's capability=y covers only SK-Masked LoRA (Table 5 MMLU/MGSM). No capability is measured under SK suppression or injection, so V1's 'other abilities kept' is untested. The Figure 3 baselines (Qwen3-8B 20.21, Llama-3.1-8B 35.98) don't match the Table 1 KO/TH/BN default averages (21.21, 40.00), and the text doesn't say why. Line 226 holds a stray Chinese author note, not an instruction.

statements.problem: none. For this study it correctly says the multilingual suppression results zero coordinate sets, not a residual direction.

statements.correction: Moved object: the equal-weight average of the EN and ZH mean SK activations during safe-response generation, added at alpha=4 to SK coordinates on KO/TH/BN inputs. The SK is the intersection of top-5000 SCAR sets from EN, ZH, IT, KO, TH and BN. Average target ASR: Qwen3-8B 20.21->11.96, Llama-3.1-8B 35.98->30.69, Gemma-2-9B-it 5.18->3.17. The authors say the magnitude varies across models while the direction is consistent.
statements.problem: The Llama-3.1-8B numbers 35.98->30.69 at alpha=4 are right. But the moved object here is not 'SK neuron coordinates'. The coordinates stay fixed and were selected with all six languages' data, including the KO/TH/BN targets, and only an activation state is transferred. The 'higher-resource' framing does not fit either: the targets include Bengali, and the text does not classify the languages.

statements.correction: r27/r30: zeroing SK FFN output coordinates (0.12% Qwen3-8B, 0.15% Llama-3.1-8B) raises six-language average MultiJail ASR 16.40->69.05 and 26.51->71.64. The transfer results are r31-r33: an EN/ZH mean safe-response activation state added on SK coordinates for KO/TH/BN inputs.
statements.problem: r27 and r30 are not transfer results. They zero the shared SK coordinates and report six-language average ASR. The study's cross-language transfer is r31-r33. The core point, that this study moves something other than a difference-in-means direction, is right.
